name: EQ for balance in three questions: what is the focus, is the clash static or dynamic (sidechained dynamic EQ), and where in the stereo field (mid-only)
goal: Resolve frequency competition between a focus element (for example a lead vocal) and other loud parts (lead synth, mid bass, piano) with a three-question framework instead of a fixed EQ scoop. (1) Name the section's focus and which parts still compete with it. (2) If the overlap changes with the focus's level, notes and pauses, use a dynamic EQ on the competing part with the focus as its sidechain key, so cuts follow the focus. (3) If the focus is mono but the competitor is stereo, run that dynamic EQ in mid-only mode so the sides keep their full level. Delta vs generic sidechain/EQ skills: the decision order and the mid-only dynamic cut.

source.title: I HATED Mixing Until I Learned This Hack
source.transcript_note: Show-transcript text; banter and end-screen CTA dropped. The video gives no numeric dynamic-EQ settings; the static '5 dB scoop' is cited only as the approach to avoid.

prerequisites: A DAW mix with a clear focus element
A dynamic EQ / resonance suppressor with an external sidechain (the video uses a commercial one and a free student-made one)
For step 3: mid/side mode on that dynamic EQ, or a mid/side encode-decode around a non-M/S dynamic EQ

inputs.name: focus_track
inputs.description: Priority element of the section (vocal in the video)

inputs.name: competing_tracks
inputs.description: Louder supporting parts overlapping the focus (lead, mid bass, piano)

outputs.name: dynamic_eq_inserts
outputs.description: A sidechain-keyed dynamic EQ on each competing track, mid-only where the focus is mono

constraints: Reach for EQ after volume balance, panning and compression have been considered
Avoid static fixed-frequency scoops for problems that change over time: they stay on during pauses, ignore level changes and miss the singer's moving notes, which over-processes the part
Works for any pair (synth vs synth, drums vs synth), not only vocals
Not affiliated with any plugin vendor

steps.action: Set general volume, stereo placement and compression first; EQ for balance comes after those.
steps.expect: Remaining clashes are frequency masking, not level problems

steps.action: Ask what the focus of this section is and which other sounds still compete with it (often the parts you chose to mix louder).
steps.expect: A short list of focus/competitor pairs, for example vocal vs arp lead

steps.action: For each pair, ask whether the overlap is static or dynamic: does it change when the focus pauses, gets louder or quieter, or moves to different notes?

For a dynamic clash, insert a dynamic EQ on the competitor and set its sidechain input to the focus track. Adjust the depth (how drastic), resolution (detailed vs broad) and any frequency ranges to ignore.
steps.expect: The competitor dips only at the focus's current frequencies and only while it sounds; it is untouched between phrases

steps.action: Ask where in the stereo field the clash happens. If the focus is mono (centre) and the competitor is stereo, switch the dynamic EQ to mid-only (or wrap it in M/S encode/decode) so only the centre is ducked.
steps.expect: The competitor's sides keep their full level and width; the centre clears for the focus

steps.action: A/B against a static scoop: compare the competitor's level and life in the focus's pauses and in its side channel.
steps.expect: The dynamic mid-only version keeps more level and power in the competitor while the focus stays clear

verification: Metered: during the focus's pauses the competitor has ~0 dB gain reduction
On a side-channel meter, the competitor's side level is unchanged with the processing on and off
The focus stays intelligible in the busiest section at the same fader levels
